title: Generation of iPSC-based human-mouse microglial brain chimeras to study senescence of human microglia
protocol: Anesthetize P0, sex unspecified neonatal pups via hypothermia: Place pups (within 24 h of birth) in protective latex sleeves.
Immerse up to the neck in crushed ice (4°C).
Wait for a 4–5 min induction time.
Anesthetize the pups by pinching their tails until no movement is observed.
Fix the heads of the pups on a stereotaxic device equipped with a neonatal mouse adaptor.
Load cells into the Hamilton syringe (5-6 μL for each pup).
Insert the needle directly through the skull to the hippocampus injection sites using a digital stereotaxic device.
Inject 0.5 μl of cell suspension into each site, totaling four injection sites per pup.
Keep the needle at each depth (1.5 mm and 1.2 mm) for at least one minute following injection.
After cell transplantation, place pups on a heating pad at 37°C for about 5-10 minutes to recover.
Return recovered pups to their dams.
Make sure the pups are warm, pink, breathing, and capable of spontaneous movements before returning them to the dam.
At 4-5 months post-transplantation, immunostain with a human-specific marker expressed by microglia (hCD45) to examine the distribution of microglia.
At 3 months post-transplantation, perform immunostaining to show the wide distribution of xenografted, hTMEM119+ human microglia in the hippocampal region.
At six months post-transplantation, analyze chimeric brains using scRNA-seq to determine the percentage of donor-derived human microglia.
Stain with hTMEM119/PSD95 or hTMEM119/CD68/PSD95 to examine synaptic pruning and phagocytic function of microglia.
Use chimeras for studying functional synaptic neurotransmission by performing patch-clamp recording of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs).
Study long-term synaptic plasticity in hippocampal slices from microglial chimeric mice at 3 months post-transplantation by inducing long-term potentiation (LTP).
Weigh the mice and calculate the appropriate dose for anesthesia.
Dilute ketamine with 0.9% saline to make an 80 mg/mL solution.
Dilute xylazine with 0.9% saline to make an 8 mg/mL solution.
Mix diluted ketamine and xylazine at a ratio of 1:1.
Inject the ketamine/xylazine mixture intraperitoneally at 0.01 mL/g of body weight.
Place the animal on a heating pad immediately after injection.
Confirm effective anesthesia by pinching the tail within 10 minutes.
Shave the fur on the skull and clean the skin with an iodine-based wash.
Inject bupivacaine subcutaneously along the incision line at 2 mg/kg.
Make a straight midline incision through the skin from the back of the neck to the interpupillary line.
Place the animal on the platform of the stereotaxic apparatus.
Fix the head with ear bars.
Use bregma as the reference (stereotaxic zero) for X and Y coordinates.
Mark the intended sites of injection on the skull at 2.0 mm bilaterally from the midline and 2.5 mm posterior to bregma.
Adjust the drill to 20,000 rpm.
Make a single burr-hole in the skull at the marked injection site.
Load pathological tau proteins into the Hamilton syringe (7–8 μL at a concentration of 0.8 μg protein/μL).
Position the syringe over the burr-hole.
Inject the fluid into two depths in the hippocampus: 1.8 mm and 2.4 mm on both sides of the mouse brain.
Inject the fluid slowly (1 μL each depth, total 4 μL per mouse) to avoid an acute increase of intracranial pressure.
Allow a minimum of 1 additional minute rest time before withdrawing the syringe from the brain.
Pull the edges of the skin together and suture the skin at 3 separate points.
Place the animal in a temperature-controlled cage until complete recovery.
Administer analgesic treatment once the animal recovers.
Monitor the injected mice every day for the first week.
Sample chimeric mice from each batch of cell transplantation experiments before tau injection.
Confirm wide microglia distribution in the sampled mice.
At two weeks post-injection, examine AT8+ p-tau distribution in mouse brains that received DSAD tau.
Examine phagocytosis of p-tau by double-staining p-tau with human microglia at 1–2 months post-tau injection.
Assess hTMEM119+ DS microglia for engulfment of AT8+ or PHF-1+ p-tau in the DSAD Tau injection group.
Compare few p-tau observed in DS microglia in the Cont tau injection group with those in the DSAD Tau group.
Use both control and DS microglial chimeras to study senescence of human microglia in vivo.
Observe senescent phenotypes such as beading, shortened processes, and fragmentation morphological changes in DS chimeric brains injected with soluble tau at 8 weeks post-transplantation.
Increase number of ferritin+/hCD45+ DS microglia is noted in the DS chimeric brains injected with soluble tau at 8 weeks.
In control microglial chimeras, observe the presence of senescent phenotypes in a small number of control microglia at 2 months post-injection of pathological tau proteins.
At 6 months post-injection of pathological tau proteins, significantly more senescent phenotypes are observed in control microglia.
After two months of tau injection, perfuse mice with ice-cold PBS.
Dissect the whole brain from the mice.
Remove the cerebellum from the dissected brain.
Perform tissue dissociation using the Adult Brain Dissociation Kit and the gentleMACS Octo Dissociator with Heaters according to manufacturer instructions.
Resuspend cell pellets in 160 μL MACS buffer (0.5% BSA in 1× PBS) + 40 μL Mouse cell removal beads.
Incubate the samples at 4°C for 15 min.
Isolate the resulting samples using LS columns and the MidiMACS™ separator.
Collect human cells from the flow-through.
Pellet the cells by centrifugation (10 min, 400g, 4°C).
Resuspend the cells to 1,000 cells per microliter in MACS buffer for scRNA-seq library preparation.
